measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes (denied ÷ originated + approved-not-accepted + denied)
statement: In 2025, Black mortgage applicants were denied 1.8× as often as white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Pulled 2026-11-19 from the Data Browser API (nationwide aggregations, races + actions_taken 1,2,3). Counts: Black 462,242 / 36,040 / 273,650; White 4,592,966 / 255,605 / 1,227,688. "White" includes Hispanic white. Raw rates, no controls for income, debt or credit. The API allows only 2 filters, so this cannot be narrowed to conventional home-purchase loans (the measure in loan-black-denial-2023); use the loan-level file for that. 2024 was 36.7% vs 21.8%.

statement: Even after comparing applicants at the same lender with similar finances, Black applicants were 7.8 percentage points more likely to be denied a mortgage than white applicants (2018–2024).

notes: Published May 2026; HMDA 2018–2024 with lender and financial controls. Figure taken from data-sources.md; open the article to confirm the table before verifying.

statement: Same-sex couples applying together were 73% more likely to be denied a mortgage than different-sex couples, and paid higher fees, though they did not default more often.
source_title: Sun, Hua, and Lei Gao, "Lending Practices to Same-Sex Borrowers," PNAS
notes: HMDA 1990–2015, same-sex couples inferred from co-applicant sex. Old data, but it is the newest national study for LGBTQ+ mortgage access. Year = publication year.

statement: In 83,000+ fake applications to 108 of the largest US employers, applicants with Black-sounding names were contacted 2.1 percentage points less often than identical applicants with white-sounding names, and the gap was concentrated in a small set of firms.
source_title: Kline, Patrick, Evan K. Rose, and Christopher R. Walters, "Systemic Discrimination Among Large U.S. Employers," QJE
notes: Data 2019–2021; published 2022. Newest large US résumé audit on race. Open the paper for the two contact rates before turning this into a normal fact.

statement: In a 2023 survey, 23% of LGBTQ workers said they had not been hired because of their sexual orientation or gender identity, and 21% said they had been fired for it.
source_title: Williams Institute, UCLA, "LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment"
notes: Survey of 1,902 LGBTQ adults, summer 2023; published Aug 2024. Lifetime: 47% discrimination or harassment at work; past year: 17%. Self-report, not an audit.

measure: share who ever experienced employment discrimination
statement: In a 2023 survey, 55% of transgender and nonbinary workers said they had faced discrimination at work, compared with 31% of cisgender lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer workers.
source_title: Williams Institute, UCLA, "LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment"
notes: Past year: 22% vs 9%. The source groups trans and nonbinary together, so this could also be tagged gender:nonbinary. Comparison group is LGBQ, not all workers.

measure: share who ever experienced employment discrimination
statement: In a 2023 survey, 42% of LGBTQ people of color said they had faced discrimination at work, compared with 27% of white LGBTQ people.
source_title: Williams Institute, UCLA, "LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment"
notes: "People of color" is all non-white groups together; race:multi is a placeholder tag, so pick the right tag (or a new one) before merging. Past year: 15% vs 7%.

statement: In an audit of 14 language models screening 24,024 paired résumés each, a 2023 model favored white names by 2.1 points, but every model released in 2024 or later showed no gap or favored Black names (up to 3.0 points). The same pattern held for gender.
source_title: Gao, Zhenyu, Wenxi Jiang, and Yutong Yan, "Can LLMs Hire Fairly? Racial Bias in Resume Screening," arXiv:2606.28978
notes: Preprint (June 2026), not yet peer-reviewed, so the README rule for findings (peer-reviewed or official) is not met yet. Newest result; it updates the 2024 Bloomberg and Wilson & Caliskan results, which tested older models.

statement: In 40,000+ applications to 13,000+ jobs, applicants age 64–66 got fewer callbacks than applicants age 29–31, and the gap was strongest for older women.
source_title: Neumark, David, Ian Burn, and Patrick Button, "Is It Harder for Older Workers to Find Jobs? New and Improved Evidence from a Field Experiment," JPE
notes: Newest large US age audit (data 2015). Free version: NBER w21669. Take the callback rates from the paper to make a normal fact.
